claims.overstatement: No overstatement; the claim understates the source in one respect. It presents the cross-sectional evidence only as 'negative correlations in three studies in one paper by the author's team' (Kite, Pearson & Henson, 2013), whereas the review states that nearly every included study found that students reporting more strategies also reported drinking less and/or fewer problems (Introduction › Protective Behavioral Strategies, 2nd paragraph; Highlights), and the author ends by calling PBS use a promising way to reduce drinking and its consequences (Conclusion). The 'insufficient' judgment on whether more strategies lower drinking is consistent with the review's own 'mixed evidence' for prospective and mediation findings, but the claim should say that the same-sitting association is reported as near-universal and that the author's reading is more favourable. Small precision points: in Luebbe et al. (2009) strategy use was unrelated to both drinking and problems at the same time point (baseline and 4 months), not only to drinking; in Larimer et al. (2007) the intervention effect was described as fully, not partly, mediated; in Martens et al. (2011) prospective correlations with drinking were similar to the cross-sectional ones (only those with problems were weaker); one of the two day-by-day studies (Lewis et al., 2012) used 7-day recall at one sitting.
claims.note: Numbers checked: 62 studies; searches ended early February 2013; at least 11 measures; 80% (Abstract only, not derived in the body); 3 moderation studies (Benton 2004, Benton 2006, Borden 2011); 3 of 9 prospective correlations non-significant; 15-day diary, n = 40; 3 mediating trials and 3 trials without change in strategy use; 1 instruction experiment. Editors' count from the Appendix recomputed: studies with a trial, experiment, follow-up or daily design are 14 definite (nos. 2, 7, 12, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35, 36, 37, 47, 52, 55, 56) plus 2 ambiguous (26, 7-day recall; 38, pre- and post-matriculation in a sample the Appendix calls cross-sectional), so 46 to 48 of 62 otherwise, 74.2% to 77.4%: same as the claim's 74% to 77%. No advice on amounts or timing; strategies appear as studied behaviours.

claims.overstatement: Not supported as worded: (1) the opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines had a lower in-treatment death rate (1.31 against 1.79) than those without benzodiazepine prescribing only; the review gives no in-treatment rate for the briefly prescribed group in the text, and Table 1 says patients with occasional benzodiazepine prescriptions had the lowest in-treatment mortality, so 'than the others' is wrong for that group. (2) 'Most drug-checking sources tested how well laboratory methods detect benzodiazepines': by Table 1, 5 or 6 of the 11 evaluated detection (Borden, Gozdzialski, Laxton, Mullin [50], Laing, partly Tobias), mostly point-of-care or portable instruments checked against laboratory confirmation; the rest report what services found, behaviour after test strips (Park, Gelberg) or users' views (Reed). Say 'about half ... point-of-care and laboratory methods'. (3) In the magnitude, 'benzodiazepine-type drugs in 116 of 555 samples, 15 of them expected to be benzodiazepines': the 15 are of the 555; the review does not say how many of the 116 were among them. Understatement: the claim omits the one observational study with numbers on behaviour after drug checking (Gelberg et al., 541 adults: a positive test-strip result went with using less, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, a reduction in quantity used reported as 20-fold when benzodiazepines were tested, which the Results word causally), and omits that the authors themselves describe drug checking as having consistent positive outcomes; the 'insufficient' judgment is the editors' and is justified by the designs, but the authors' reading should be shown as theirs. Minor: 'most often together with opioids, stimulants or alcohol' is not quantified in the review; the isolation-hotel source (Brothers et al.) is a medRxiv preprint. No dosing or administration guidance in the claim (the review's '50% of usual dose' and 'up to 30 mg daily' are rightly omitted).
claims.note: Numbers checked against Table 1 and text: 35 sources; groups 11, 5, 9, 10; designs recounted from Table 1: 17 quantitative, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews (one a rapid review), 1 policy analysis, no randomized trial (the Results text's own breakdown, 20/1/4/2/1, adds to 28). 59 samples, 36%, 78%, 9%, 62%; 11 of 15; 33/139 = 23.7%; 2, 4 and 14 of 20; 116 and 15 of 555; 24 (41%); 68 of 103, 96% to 68%, 22% to 7%, 69%; 6 of 77; more than 70; 278, 127, 72/34/51 months, 1.31/1.79, 450% to 5.90 (5.90/1.31 = 4.50, an increase of 350%: editors' calculation reproduced); 4 of 5; 57 to 23 (-59.6%) and 160 to 238 (+48.8%), cited from reference 82, a two-page response letter (Lloyd et al., 2017); 89% (Kentucky, six clinics); 183/1112 = 16.5%; 6635/17,616 = 37.7%. Search rerun on 7 July 2025 confirmed. 'Presence, not cause' and 'involved' wording respected.

claims.overstatement: Not supported as worded: 'The only numbers come from a before-and-after pilot' (statement) and 'No comparison and no effect estimate' (magnitude). The review also reports Gelberg et al. (541 adults who use drugs, 28 days, observational): after a positive fentanyl test-strip result people reported using smaller amounts, taking turns and having naloxone nearby, with the reduction in quantity used reported as four-fold overall and 20-fold when benzodiazepines were tested (Results › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph, in causal wording; Table 1, as an association). It compares behaviour after positive against negative results among people who test, not people who used a practice against people who did not, and its outcome is behaviour, not harm, so the claim's 'no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not' still stands. If added, it should be reported as an association with reported quantity, without amounts. Minor: '(45, interviewed)': the review gives a qualitative study of 45 but does not say interviews. The claim correctly leaves out the forum's dosing and frequency details, the 'tester shot' and 'smaller amount' examples and the end-of-day timing in the ethnography.
claims.note: Checked: flubromazolam forum (Andersson and Kjellgren, qualitative, N = 122 in Table 1) and the five practices named; British Columbia women and gender-diverse people (Speed et al., qualitative, 45); Melbourne ethnography (Dwyer, one participant); Bangkok survey of 252 (Kerr et al., education to avoid injecting alone); Baltimore pilot 68 of 103, 69%, 96% to 68%; Limitations (term-based search; peer-led resources not covered); Conclusions (absence for people not seeking abstinence or treatment). Borden et al. adds unquantified accounts ('several' samples returned for destruction; smaller doses, not using alone, carrying naloxone reported).

claims.overstatement: No overstatement; the claim keeps association language, separates the coroners' background figures from the study's data and states the sampling limit. Two precision points: (1) 'Offered a short list of reasons ... the 314 most often chose ...' lists five reasons, but two of them (having no one to use with; not wanting to share or cheaper) were not offered options: they are themes the authors coded from free-text 'other' answers (Table 3, footnote a), so their shares are not comparable with the offered options and are probably undercounts; say so. (2) 'in 2019 more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths happened in a private residence': the paper says the place of injury was determined to be a private residence. 'Coroners' reports' is right: references 9 and 13 are British Columbia Coroners Service reports.
claims.note: All numbers found as printed. Recomputed: 314/414 = 75.8%, Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7% (same as the claim); 198/414 = 47.8%; 139/314 = 44.3% and 139/264 = 52.7%; 264 = 314 - 31 - 19; 44/314 = 14.0%; 37/314 = 11.8% (printed 11.7%); 30/314 = 9.6%; 27/314 = 8.6%. The 414 are the 486 who completed the survey less 37 missing and 35 prefer-not-to-say answers on using alone. 'Alone' is not defined in the question. The overdose item is an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months. No advice on amounts, timing or routes (the Background's public-health messages on amounts and pace are rightly not repeated).

claims.overstatement: No material overstatement; the claim follows the Table rather than the abstract and keeps 'associated with' and the attribution caveats. Small wording points: (1) the statement's 'Peak ratings on 0-100 scales' are peak changes from each session's baseline (the magnitude says so correctly); (2) 'without knowing which brownie they had eaten' rests on the double-blind design, and the paper reports no check of blinding; (3) 'divided-attention error' is the mean distance of the cursor from the moving target (higher is worse; units not printed); (4) the magnitude's 'printed Cohen's d values for the effects do not match the printed means and SDs' is true of several but not all (drug effect 0.5, memory 0.3, routine tasks 0.6 and the THC and 11-OH-THC Cmax and AUC values agree with a pooled-SD calculation). No dosing or potentiation guidance: doses appear as study conditions.
claims.note: All numbers in statement and magnitude found as printed. Editors' arithmetic recomputed: THC Cmax 14.8/8.2 = 1.80, AUC 84.9/33.3 = 2.55; 11-OH-THC Cmax 53.9/4.5 = 11.98, AUC 349.0/34.0 = 10.26; same as the claim (about 1.8, 2.5, 12, 10). Every pair the claim calls significant carries the Table's c marker (Tukey P < .05 between active conditions); anxious, paranoid, sleepy, pleasant and liking carry no c marker. The text prints dry or red eyes after the CBD-dominant extract as 28.7, the Table 28.8. Peak-time values are means of individual peak times; their ranges never exceed 6.0 h although assessments ran to 24 h; no test of peak time is reported. Duration of the stronger effects: only in Figures 3 and 4, which were not viewable, so the claim's 'not given in the parts that could be read' stands.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low follows from unmet critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 13, all consistent with the full text (PubMed only, 4 of 14 added ad hoc, no risk-of-bias tool, no protocol).

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits; the quoted Conclusion phrase is exact. One nuance in the card's analysis field (not a key finding): 'absorption was equally associated with challenging experiences' overstates slightly; in Haijen 2018 the coefficient was 0.215 for challenge against 0.347 for mystical-type.

missed: The card's exposure field calls both Russ 2019 studies 'online samples'; the review never says so for those studies, and the only basis in the review is the general Limitations remark about retrospective designs using online crowd-sourcing (true or not of the primary studies, it is not stated in this source).

Table 2's openness row cites ref. 54 (Haijen 2018) alongside 46 and 48, although none of the outcomes listed there (adverse experience, oceanic boundlessness, mystical experience) come from Haijen; a further citation mismatch in the same family as reporting issues 1 to 4 and 8.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: The Background does not say 'regardless of cause': it describes np-SAD as counting 'relevant deaths' where there is a history of drug abuse, without saying which causes count as relevant. Corrected issue: the Background includes deaths with a history of drug abuse (and Table 1 shows 25 of the 70 counted deaths were not from drug toxicity), while the Discussion says np-SAD's definition excludes deaths from bacterial and viral infections; the paper does not reconcile the two. The consequence stands.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence with an overall 'moderate' fits a description of what one local count contained. The domain notes are accurate; I confirm the domain 8 statement: each printed p-value reproduces with Fisher's exact test (residence 0.338, methadone 0.022, treatment 0.005, criminal justice 0.043) or the uncorrected chi-square test (sex 0.924, heroin/morphine 0.001, alcohol 0.339, alcohol history 0.569), and toxicity 0.002 and cocaine <0.001 with both. The Wilson intervals (30.0%, 20.5-41.5; 35.6%, 24.6-48.3; 64.3%, 52.6-74.5; 35.7%, 25.5-47.4) and the Newcombe interval (40.5 points, 15.9-57.1) reproduce exactly.

interpretation_gap.note: The card's account of the gap is right, but I would rate it moderate rather than minor. Two statements in the abstract are not results of the data: the Results say the toxicity deaths outside the drug abuser category were mainly from antidepressants, antipsychotics and analgesics, with no counts anywhere in the paper; and the Conclusion says the compact definitions miss deaths from blood-borne viruses, which the study did not examine (it rests on cited figures). The Discussion also calls 21 of 70 deaths 'large numbers'. The main conclusion (the count includes deaths outside np-SAD's drug abuser category) is supported.

missed: Methods name the criminal-justice databases as Drug Arrest Referral 2003/04 and the Drug Interventions Programme 2004/05, but the Table 1 row and footnote 3 cover 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06 (Drug Interventions Programme 2004/05 and 2005/06). This minor inconsistency is not recorded, and the card's design_detail gives only the Methods version.

selection_effects says Liverpool had the highest count 'in England and Wales'; the paper says the area of the UK with the highest reported number in 2004 (Background, 2nd paragraph; Abstract, Background).
KF10 / interpretation gap: the 4% cirrhosis figure is from a Scottish modelling study (reference 11), applied by the authors to the UK.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high, for the reallocated estimate, as the card reasons. Low risk only for what the certificates say. Item judgments checked; item 8's 'internally consistent' rates confirmed (no percentage change differs from the recomputation by more than 1 point).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The Conclusions' 'have been missed' is firmer than the body's 'could be categorized'; the card records this.

missed: The rates in Table 2 are not described as crude or age-adjusted, and no population source is named. The populations implied by the table (for example 261 deaths at 5.37 per 100,000 gives 4.86 million for Alabama) fit 2015 state populations, so the rates appear crude and should not be set beside CDC's age-adjusted rates.

Discussion, 4th paragraph: Kentucky's opioid codes rising 43% and unspecified reporting falling 28% over 1999–2015 (points or relative change not stated) are read as showing that 'state-based efforts can improve' drug-specific reporting. This is a before-and-after trend in one state with no comparison.

Correction (funding.affiliations_note): two authors are at the University of Pittsburgh Graduate School of Public Health, but only Buchanich is listed in the Department of Biostatistics (Burke's affiliation is the school). For Williams the article gives only the Office of the Medical Examiner of Allegheny County; that he certifies deaths is not stated in the article.

Context for the replication timeline: Buchanich is a co-author of the Slavova et al. 2019 review that relays this paper's 70,000 estimate (card sc_slavova_2019), so that review is not independent support.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; overall some concerns, not milder than the worst domain.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. Small precision point in results_show: 'ratios from about 0.7' fits only the two carbon monoxide deaths (25-30% lower), or the chloroquine figure, which is ante-mortem:post-mortem (post-mortem:ante-mortem about 1.4). Every drug ratio the review lists is 1.0 (salicylate) or higher, so the human drug data run one way (higher after death). The Conclusion's 'no reliable or obvious connection' is broader than examples that include ratios near 1 (salicylate 1.0, paracetamol 1.5, moclobemide little redistribution).

missed: Internal inconsistency in the Rouzioux figures. Site-related and time-related differences, 1st paragraph: 8 of 10 cases had post-mortem left-ventricular concentrations 2.58 to 17.66 times those in life. Relationship..., 1st paragraph lists imipramine 1.39 for the same series, below that minimum; sample timing or site may differ but is not stated. The card repeats both (key finding 6; 1980 timeline entry) without noting the conflict.

The card calls Ritter the journal's Editor-in-Chief (design_detail, affiliations_note; 'the journal's editor' in where_it_stands). Neither PMC page states this: the piece is labelled EDITORIAL, written in the journal's 'we publish' voice, with a King's College London affiliation. Source the title or say 'the journal's editorial'.

risk_of_bias.note: The editors' evidence-report checklist read as a statistics report, with an overall 'some concerns', fits. The tables are internally consistent (I reproduced every percentage in Tables A, B and C), and the problems are in the Discussion's wording and the notes, as the card says. The card never turns 'mentioned' or 'involved' into 'caused'.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The abstract's 'stabilized' for a 1.8% fall (22.7 to 22.3) that the Table calls significant is a fair lay summary; the substantive conflicts are inside the Discussion and are all listed.

missed: Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 3rd paragraph, lists methamphetamine among drugs with steep increases from 2017 to 2023. The Results and Table footnote 6 give a significant increase only for 2017-2021, with the rate stable from 2021 (9.7) to 2023 (10.4). This is a sixth example of the Discussion going beyond its tables, in the same paragraph as gaps 1 to 3.

Results › Drug overdose deaths in 2023 involving multiple drugs, 2nd paragraph, calls methamphetamine the second or third most frequent concomitant drug 'among the other top drugs'. For oxycodone, Table B gives alprazolam (19.1%) and cocaine (17.2%) as second and third, so methamphetamine is not in the top three for every drug. Minor.

Locator consistency (findings 5 and 7, and the interpretation gap's 'Data considerations, 5th and 6th paragraphs'): these numbers count the bulleted list as a paragraph. Running-text-only counting gives 4th and 5th. Worth fixing one way for all readers' anchors.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Standard 2 says admission blood and urine are to be collected and tested 'as opposed to' autopsy specimens, when applicable and available. The card's '(not only autopsy)' turns a preference into an addition. Corrected: test admission rather than autopsy blood and urine where applicable and available. The other eight points match.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: 'Without explanation' is too strong. Case 2 itself gives no reason, but its scenario (methadone started 4 days earlier) is the one the 2nd paragraph of the causality section describes: long half-life drugs such as methadone accumulating to toxic concentrations in the first days of treatment, before steady state or tolerance. The comment speaks of tolerance to 'the drug's effects', meaning methadone. Corrected issue: Case 2 does not explain why years of other opioid analgesics conferred no tolerance to methadone (the induction-period rationale is left implicit). In both cases tolerance is inferred from history, not measured, and in both the inference supports attribution. The consequence stands.

risk_of_bias.note: The editors' narrative-review checklist with an overall 'high' fits, since no recommendation is linked to graded evidence. I checked the domain-3 note: reference 5 has co-chair Goldberger as an author and reference 14 is panel member Hanzlick's book. The reasoning's limits on what the statement may be cited for are right.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair for a consensus statement. One reading point: the Conclusions sentence ('Concise, scientifically accurately, universally accepted case definitions like those presented here can address...') can also be read as aspirational (definitions of this kind, once accepted, could address the distinction), so 'no evidence of acceptance is offered' should be framed as a possible overstatement rather than a plain claim of acceptance.

missed: The scene-investigation recommendations appear only in the exposure field, not as a key finding: inventory the drugs at the scene to estimate the amount taken; for controlled prescription drugs, request the state prescription-monitoring records (prescription history, use without a prescription, tolerance); in methadone or buprenorphine deaths, contact local opioid treatment programmes (Scene Investigation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). They bear directly on how a death is investigated, one of the new section's questions.

Standard 2 recommends testing admission (pre-death) specimens, while the drug-detected definition is built on post-mortem testing and excludes deaths whose toxicology was done before death by hospital staff. The statement does not say whether a drug found only in admission specimens tested by the medical examiner's laboratory makes a death drug-detected.

Toxicologic Testing, 3rd paragraph: the panel asks that measurements be judged on whether they can separate acute from chronic use (free against glucuronidated metabolites, by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry). This is not in the card's findings.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high (appraisal and balance domains high). Reliance on own studies 'low' checked: no review author is among the named authors of refs 17 and 31–46 (refs 31 and 45 end in et al.).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, at its upper edge: the abstract says 'Across studies', but the 20–35% range is printed for one study (Ruhm 2018). Recomputed the card's editors' calculation: 1 − 1/1.20 = 16.7% and 1 − 1/1.35 = 25.9%, so about 17–26% (17.4% from the 21% lower bound for any opioid).

missed: Lowder (Table 2): the review says adding toxicology 'doubled' the opioid-involved share from 34.2% to 86.0%; that is a 2.5-fold rise (86.0/34.2 = 2.51), and the 642 added cases were recoded because an opioid was found in toxicology, which shows presence, not cause.

Results › 2 says the state and county studies covered seven states across the Northeast, South and West, but one of the seven is Indiana (Marion County), in the Midwest. The seven are California, Maryland, Florida, New York, Pennsylvania, Kentucky and Indiana.

Discussion, 1st paragraph calls the national 20–35% 'consistent with studies at the state level' (refs 40, 41). These are different measures. Horon's 26% is additional heroin-related deaths as a share of all overdose deaths. Quast's 34% is additional opioid-related deaths as a share of the NVSS count. Neither is a corrected opioid count comparable with Ruhm's.
Minor citation and spelling errors: Hurstak is dated 2017 in Table 3 and 2018 in the reference list (ref 31); 'Statitistics' (ref 3); SAMHSA misnamed (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

Figure 1 (PRISMA): image not viewable in my tab either; the 66% of imported records removed as duplicates (Discussion, 6th paragraph) implies about 344 records imported (117/0.34), which only the figure could confirm.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high is justified by unadjusted confounding (drug type, psychiatric history, other drugs) and heavy unanalysed attrition (about 198 of 654 in the acute-experience model).

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits: causal verbs in the Abstract ('promoted', 'decrease the likelihood'), the Strengths claim about causal inference, the unsupported variance statement, and Implications turning associations into recommendations. Quoted Discussion phrase checked against the source.

missed: Discussion, 2nd paragraph: lifetime number of psychedelic uses correlated negatively with the change in well-being, r(279) = -0.23, p < 0.001 (people with more experience improved less), consistent with the lifetime-uses x time interaction in Table 6; relevant wherever the well-being rise is cited.

Discussion > Strengths, 1st paragraph: the authors describe the design as never before implemented in psychedelic research (as of 2018); the claims' 'the one prospective study' framing rests on this plus the editors' own knowledge of the literature, which the card could note under replication.

risk_of_bias.note: Moderate (editors' summary; JBI has no overall algorithm). This is consistent with the difference from buchanich_2018: here each added death rests on that death's own toxicology or scene record, not on an assumed proportion. The protocol, however, is unvalidated, partly presence-based, and was applied by the producing agencies with reviewers not reported. Item 8 checked: the intervals are Wald-type and reproduce.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. Gap (5) checked: the editorial's passages naming this study summarize it as showing that standard certificates may underestimate heroin deaths and that enhanced surveillance can better identify heroin, with no comment on the method.

missed: Reporting issue: the SAMHSA recommendations in DISCUSSION, 7th paragraph (list every physiologically significant drug, name the parent drug rather than the metabolite, avoid 'overdose' and 'use', judge whether toxicology separates chronic from acute use) are cited to ref 12, the 2015 Maryland Vital Statistics Annual Report. The SAMHSA panel paper is ref 10. The card's replication timeline says this recommendation is cited as ref 10. Correct it to 'printed as ref 12, presumably meant ref 10'.

RESULTS, 3rd paragraph calls the Table 3 figures 'the percentage of overdose death records reporting heroin'. They are the share of protocol-defined heroin deaths whose certificate named heroin, a sensitivity against the enhanced definition, not a share of all overdose deaths. The card's findings word this correctly; the paper's wording should not be copied into claims.

DISCUSSION, 8th paragraph links the rise from 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015) to implementation of these recommendations being under way in Maryland, but gives no data on implementation. This is a trend read as an effect.

Addition to funding.affiliations_note: by the CONTRIBUTORS note, Fowler (the chief medical examiner) contributed to data collection and to the study's conception and design, and Horon to data collection, analysis and interpretation. So the certifying office helped both build and apply the protocol.

Correction (cannot_establish): 'no independent reference standard or second reviewer was used'. The paper does not report who reviewed the records or how many reviewers there were, so 'second reviewer not reported' is accurate. The card's exposure field already words it that way.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high: two high domains (confounding by overall session quality; an exposure rated from interviews at the outcome visit) that could each produce the association, which fits ROBINS-E's rule for very high when several high domains substantially lower confidence.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial (arguably severe): 'central mediating role' and 'outcomes suffered' rest on uncontrolled, unadjusted correlations in 19 patients with no mediation test; the limitations paragraph concedes the causal problem.

missed: Minor: self-rated drug intensity correlated with none of the three music ratings (Results > Inter-rating reliability and discriminative validity of music experience variables, 1st paragraph), the authors' basis for treating music experience as distinct from drug intensity; not among the key findings.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Replace 'only one had a control group' with: only one compared music with no music (Kim et al., 2010); the review's Table 1 records a control group for the Breeksema interview study without saying how many listened to music, and the other three had no control group. The rest of the finding (46 children; 12/8/3 recordings; outcomes; the other four studies) is confirmed.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high under the editors' review checklist (none-applicable), following the two high domains: no appraisal of included studies, and benefits stated as findings in the highlights and recommendations.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: highlights, 3.3, 3.4 and a recommendation state effects the limitations say cannot be concluded.

missed: The abstract and introduction (4th paragraph) say the extant studies include healthy volunteers, but none of the 14 included studies did (Tables 1 and 2); every included study was in patients in clinical or trial settings.
Minor: Table 1 (Pereira row) says 'open-label ketamine' for the phase after the double-blind esketamine period, apparently a slip for esketamine.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The class ranges are the Discussion's (3rd paragraph), and Table 2 contradicts them. Trazodone, an antidepressant, has a ratio of 0.57, and dixyrazine, a phenothiazine antipsychotic, 0.33: both fall below the stated ranges for the other drugs of their class (antidepressants 1.2 to 4.7, antipsychotics 1.8 to 24). Mesoridazine (ratio 1) is also missing from the authors' list of antipsychotics at 1. Write 'the Discussion states ...' and add that by Table 2 the ranges are 0.57 to 4.7 for antidepressants and 0.33 to 24 for antipsychotics.
key_findings_flagged.note: The rest is confirmed. 'Most' neutral and acidic drugs within or below the range holds, with exceptions (phenazepam 2.1, gabapentin 1.8, pregabalin 1.6).

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with the overall rating (editors' summary: moderate), and the JBI prevalence checklist fits a description of a measurement's distribution. Measurement quality is high; the bias lies in what the distributions are taken to represent (mixed causes of death, left-censoring at the LOQ, pathologists who knew the concentrations when certifying poisonings) and in misprints.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair: the abstract and Results are descriptive, and the overreach sits in the Conclusions. Two wording points for the card. (1) The Conclusions say the agreement is 'suggesting' that post-mortem reference concentrations apply internationally; the card's 'call ... applicable' drops that hedge. (2) results_show lists moclobemide among exceptions to the 'about 20 drugs in common', but the moclobemide difference comes from the comparison with Druid and Holmgren and Reis et al., not from the 20 drugs shared with Jones and Holmgren.

missed: Reporting issue: the Discussion's class ranges are contradicted by Table 2. Antidepressants other than fluoxetine are said to range from 1.2 to 4.7, but trazodone is 0.57. Antipsychotics are said to be 1 or from 1.8 to 24, but dixyrazine is 0.33, and mesoridazine (1) is left out of the list (Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, rows 35, 69 and 120).

Several printed ratios cannot be reproduced from the printed medians: amlodipine 0.07/0.015 = 4.7 (printed 4.5), metformin 6/1 = 6.0 (5.5), phenazepam 0.09/0.04 = 2.25 (2.1), betaxolol 0.10/0.05 = 2.0 (1.9). These were probably computed from unrounded medians. No category changes, so the counts stand, but cite ratios as printed and do not recompute them from the table.

How a case entered the data: the 57,903 cases average about 5,260 a year, against 'over 6,500' toxicology cases a year described for the system. The paper does not say which toxicology cases are missing from the femoral-blood dataset (for example bodies without femoral blood, or analyses that were not comprehensive), so deaths sampled differently may be excluded.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E some concerns overall. Five domains at some concerns sits near ROBINS-E's multiple-domain route to high; I keep some concerns because the adjusted estimate is stable (1.52-1.61) and the exposure error probably biases toward the null. It would move to high if the NVDRS/SUDORS coverage were found to differ by county type.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The most consequential element is the abstract giving 1.79 as if unadjusted and omitting the reversed pooled OR 0.32 (3.1% vs 8.9% crude).

missed: Causal verbs for associations: Results 5th paragraph (unemployment 'reduced the odds'), Results 6th paragraph (autopsy 'raised the odds'), Discussion 5th paragraph (suicide note 'reduced the odds ... by 54%'). Cross-sectional associations; the card notes only the autopsy reading.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high, agreed; no included source is by the review's authors.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. The interpretation-gap text's 'most drug-checking sources test how well analytical methods detect benzodiazepines' is borderline: 5 or 6 of 11 by Table 1.

missed: The isolation-hotel source (Brothers et al., reference 55) is cited as a 2022 medRxiv preprint, so the agonist-treatment outcome for 6 of 77 residents rests on a non-peer-reviewed report.
Table 1 (Bakker and Streel) says the occasional-prescription group had the lowest in-treatment mortality, which qualifies the maintained group's 1.31 against 1.79.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high overall follows from no adjustment at all (confounding), recalled self-weighted exposure that includes after-use practices, and survivor selection; the domain judgments match what I found.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial on the none/minor/substantial/severe scale: hedged wording, but a causal reading of r of about 0.2, a circular 'credibility' argument for the ratings, an abstract that blurs the null most-recent CEQ result, and a limitations sentence that misstates EBI by setting.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, editors' summary moderate, agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor agreed.

missed: Two of the five reported reasons (having no one to use with; not wanting to share or cheaper) exist only as themes coded from free-text 'other' answers, while the others were pre-printed options; the card records the recoding (key finding 7) but not that their percentages are not comparable with the offered options and are likely undercounts.
Age bands are labelled '> 50' in Tables 1 and 2 but described as 50 or older in the text (minor).

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall some concerns, agreed. Seven of the 62 included studies have the author as co-author, as the card says.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract and most of the body are cautious; the overreach is in the Highlights ('consistently' negative) and the final sentence, as the card states.

missed: No key finding records the review's own summary of the cross-sectional evidence: nearly every included study found that students reporting more PBS reported drinking less and/or fewer problems (Introduction › Protective Behavioral Strategies, 2nd paragraph). It sits only in the interpretation gap, and the claim omits it.

Change-score findings that favour PBS are not recorded: in a non-efficacious peer intervention, change in each PBS subscale correlated negatively with change in one to three alcohol outcomes (Cimini et al., 2009; Appendix no. 7), and in its panel follow-up Manner of Drinking change predicted fewer drinks per week at 6 and 12 months (Martens et al., 2011; Non-experimental longitudinal designs paragraph).

risk_of_bias.note: Very high overall rests on the exposure domain: retrospective, near-ceiling ratings of one's own ceremony whose items overlap the outcomes (feeling safe in the ceremony space vs extreme fear). Domain judgments match my reading.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: causal and 'verify' language for a path model chosen on the same cross-sectional data. Minor: the card's interpretation_gap and analysis fields refer to 'reporting issue 4' for the discussion's departures from the tables, which is index 3 in the 0-based array (the 4th issue).

missed: The paper gives no mean, SD or distribution for the extreme-fear item or the integration-difficulty count (or the other intermediate outcomes), so the coefficients cannot be expressed relative to their spread; only the Kessler-10 scale range allows the editors' whole-range arithmetic.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: Correction: reference 16 (Peterson et al., 2021) is titled as a review of protective-strategy measures 'and associated PBS-related interventions', not of measures only. One of the four citations is therefore a review that covers intervention studies. 'None is a trial' still holds by title, but the consequence that the analogy supplies no evidence of effect cannot be concluded from titles; those reviews would need to be read.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high: the search is stated but narrow, there are no selection criteria and nothing is appraised. The card's advice to cite the review only as a map of strategies and for the scarcity of outcome research is right.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is defensible because the abstract and implications are hedged and the conclusion asks for efficacy research. 'Moderate' would also be defensible: the abstract pools classic psychedelics with ketamine and MDMA (MDMA from a preprint), and the one classic-psychedelic outcome study is read as fewer challenging experiences. Logged as a possible domain-level difference, not an overall one.

missed: The review's sections on amounts and combinations (Results › Dosing, 1st and 2nd paragraphs: starting low, setting limits, spacing doses, cannabis alongside psychedelics, cannabis with MDMA compared with other combinations) are descriptions of what the literature reports. Any claim drawing on them must keep them as reported practices, never as advice on amounts or combinations. The claims checked in this round do so.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence; the editors' summary is high. Wilson intervals recomputed (31.7-48.9%, 44.3-71.2%, 48.4-74.8%). The count of 82 tests, 16 at p<0.05 and 4 more flagged was recounted from Tables 2-4.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One addition: the card calls the abstract's 'uptake not yet complete' restrained. Its basis is a non sequitur, though: coroners already testing before the mandate would also report no increase, and no item asked whether all decedents are tested (Discussion 1st paragraph).

missed: Discussion 2nd paragraph says experience 'affected the uptake of toxicology testing requests', and the 6th says location 'impacted the uptake'. But Table 2's more-toxicology item does not differ by years (55.6% vs 60%, p=0.76) or region (59.1% vs 57.7%, p=0.92). The uptake claims rest on attitude and barrier items.

Discussion 4th paragraph says toxicology training 'addresses the barrier of restricted space' on the certificate. Results 9th paragraph reports the opposite pattern: trained coroners cited lack of room more often (88% vs 50%).
Discussion 5th paragraph says the epidemic 'more than quadrupled coroner caseloads' with no data or citation; the survey measured only whether caseloads had risen.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high overall: no adjustment beyond mutual adjustment within each block, and exposure and outcome reported together about a recalled experience. The card rightly separates using the paper for the proportions in this sample from using it for predictors.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is defensible: 'nationally representative' and 'covariate-adjusted' in the abstract, plus the Discussion's advice on guidelines, legalization and mindfulness preparation. Against that, the language is associational throughout and the limitations paragraph states the main caveats.

missed: Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 1st paragraph: the sample size was planned from a published prevalence estimate (ref. 17), at about 395 people with lifetime use among about 2,800 respondents, which implies an expected 14.1% (editors' calculation). The panel gave 21.7%, about 1.5 times that, which points to the opt-in panel over-representing people who have used psychedelics (or to a rise in use). The card says the 21.7% was 'not compared with any national survey in the paper' and misses this comparison inside the paper.

Trivial, no consequence: Table 1 prints 8.7% for 53 people twice ('Other significant symptoms', 'Slightly disagree'), where 53 of 613 is 8.6% (apparently rounded twice); Table 2 prints '1,1' for other antipsychotic medications.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence with an overall 'moderate' fits the certificate-data comparison. Domain 4 'no' is justified: the argument turns on certification practice, which is not described for the 11 jurisdictions.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the undercount statements are hedged in the text and the practical advice follows from the data. The card rightly notes that heroin is claimed but not analysed.

missed: 11th paragraph: the commentary cites the 2013 recommendation of the National Association of Medical Examiners and American College of Medical Toxicology expert panel that certifiers list all substances responsible for a fatal overdose, and the 2013 SAMHSA uniform definitions. It says that until these are consistently adopted, counts should be read with caution where the share of unspecified deaths is considerable. The 12th paragraph adds that NCHS and some states were working to improve drug specification. Neither is a key finding, though both bear on how deaths are certified.

7th paragraph: the MCOD files are described as covering certificate data 'for U.S. citizens'. NCHS mortality files are by residence, so this is probably a slip (from my own knowledge, not stated in the source; to be confirmed). The card's population description should not repeat 'citizens'.

selection_effects says the authors 'work in the health departments of the jurisdictions they describe, including the first author's Kentucky'. The first author is at the University of Kentucky College of Public Health (Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center), not a health department, as the card's own affiliations_note says; the other ten are at health departments.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high (no systematic search) follows the worst-domain rule. One domain note needs correcting: the balance domain says over-attribution is mentioned only in Gill's remark, but the review also reports the SAMHSA panel's distinction between 'drug-caused' and 'drug-detected' deaths (MDI subsection, 4th paragraph), the rule that non-contributing drugs should not be recorded (7th paragraph) and NAME's call to interpret toxicology in the context of the circumstances (3rd paragraph). The judgment (some concerns) still fits: none of these is quantified.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. Gap (1) is weak: the abstract's claim that text tools improve specific-opioid quantification is compatible with the body's statement that they cannot reach certificates naming no drug.

missed: Correction (funding.affiliations_note): four authors are at the University of Kentucky (Slavova, Delcher, Bunn, Costich), not five; with Buchanich (Pittsburgh) and Goldberger (Florida) the article has six authors.

Correction (design_detail): Goldberger's printed affiliation is the Department of Pathology, Immunology and Laboratory Medicine, College of Medicine, University of Florida; 'forensic toxicology' describes his field, and his role as co-chair of the SAMHSA panel is not stated in this article (it may come from the Goldberger 2013 card).

Missed finding relevant to 'involved' versus 'caused': the three recommendation papers. The SAMHSA consensus panel distinguished 'drug-caused' from 'drug-detected' deaths and said non-uniform classification undermines incidence and prevalence data; NAME called for a complete scene investigation, a comprehensive toxicology panel interpreted in the context of the circumstances, all responsible substances listed by generic name, and 'accident' as the manner for opioid misuse without apparent intent of self-harm, keeping 'undetermined' for rare cases where evidence supports more than one intent; OSAC named three essential initiatives (MDI subsection, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Methodologic Considerations, 4th paragraph).

Missed finding: the relayed CSTE Overdose Subcommittee recommendation that jurisdictions be compared on total drug overdose death rates, and that drug-specific trends remain useful only while the degree of drug specification does not vary markedly from year to year (Methodologic Considerations, 2nd paragraph).

Minor: Ruhm's state-level adjusted rates (2008 to 2014) varied widely with the share of unspecified deaths, and the authors note predictive models could add ME/C jurisdiction type and toxicology protocols but such data are not readily available (Statistical Adjustment, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). The replication timeline's Garnett 2026 entry is not from this source and was not checked here.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low agreed: seven critical items are unmet. AMSTAR 2 applied by analogy is a reasonable choice for a structured search with pooled case analysis (Springer labels the paper a Review). Item 4 is 'no' from the unjustified English-only restriction alone.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed; every quoted phrase was checked against the page. On point (6): the 1-in-353,000 figure reproduces only if the 42 tons are US short tons and the upper end of the paper's assumed amount per use is taken (with metric tonnes about 1 in 389,000). The sentence gives no clear source for the roughly 2,700 deaths: it cites a drugabuse.com page for consumption and a federal drug-impaired-driving report after the risk figure. 'Commercial website' is the card's own description of the drugabuse.com reference.

missed: Reporting issue (Discussion, 1st paragraph): the authors call the 'other or unspecified' force category 'less aggressive forms of restraint (i.e. pepper spray, 4-point restraint, etc.)', but the Methods (4th paragraph) define it as also including blunt objects. The '2.5 times' figure is the inverse of Table 3's 0.4.

Reporting issue (Results › Analysis of outcome): the text says drug use differed significantly for most categories and lists alcohol and stimulants alongside cocaine, marijuana and other drugs, but Table 2 gives p = 0.26 and 0.15 for these two. Discussion, 2nd paragraph, says the marijuana and 'other' drug associations held 'regardless of diagnosis', yet no analysis stratified by label is reported.

selection_effects undercounts: by the paper's own reference titles, at least seven Table 1 sources name a death in restraint or restraint asphyxia. Adding Stratton et al. 1995 (2 cases), Rayamane et al. 2015 (2), Morrison and Sadler 2001 (1) and Kunz et al. 2018 (1) to the card's three gives 55 cases (33%), plus one in-custody death (Kennedy and Savard 2017). The critics' own figures for Stratton 2001's non-fatal cases differ (196 in 2023, 194 in 2024), which justifies the card's 'about'.

Interests: the 2023 reply also has no conflict-of-interest statement and gives Freeman's second affiliation as a post-office box in Portland, Oregon. The 2024 consultation declaration is printed under the heading 'Ethics approval and consent to participate'.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E some concerns fits. One small point: the exposure-measurement domain says personality was measured at screening; the text says so for the NEO-FFI only, the STAI-T timing is not stated (does not change the judgment).

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is defensible (accurate abstract, hedged practical conclusion), though the Discussion's 'led to' and the Conclusions' 'increased the likelihood' are causal. Gap (4) repeats the claim's 'cannot separate': with dose per kilogram ranging 0.8 to 2.7 mg/kg and two doses, sex and dose per kilogram are correlated, not inseparable; 'cannot cleanly separate' is more exact. Quoted Conclusions phrase is exact.

missed: 112 of the 194 (seven studies) also took MDMA in a second session after a medication pretreatment (Methods > Study design, 1st paragraph); the order of sessions is not given, so some MDMA-alone sessions may have followed an in-study MDMA exposure that the 'previous MDMA use' predictor does not count. Worth a line under exposure or limitations.

The 5D-ASC was completed 6 h after dosing as a retrospective rating of the session (Methods > Response variables, 4th paragraph); 'anxiety during the session' in the card and the claim is a same-day retrospective rating.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E for non-randomized between-person predictors is the right instrument despite the randomized source studies; overall some concerns fits an association question (dose-only adjustment, no study term, partly circular dose in two studies, study #8 without placebo).

interpretation_gap.note: Quoted abstract phrase is exact. The causal Discussion readings and the untested preparation and dose-sequence speculation are correctly flagged and not reproduced.

missed: Implication of key finding 3 not drawn: by the Results text (4th paragraph) pre-drug well-being was significantly associated with every subjective scale except VAS bad drug effect, changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood, which includes 5D-ASC anxious ego dissolution and anxiety, and the Discussion (1st paragraph) says effects were more pronounced with higher well-being and also with higher pre-drug anxiety. So in these data a better mood went with stronger effects generally, including anxiety-type scales, rather than with a less challenging session (sign for those scales is in Fig. 1, not viewable). Claims using Vizeli as support for 'better state of mind, less challenging experience' should say so.

Discussion, 7th paragraph: 'although all but one of the analyzed studies included a placebo session' is a second place where the paper itself states the 8/9 fact, worth adding to reporting issue 1's locator.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high for Study 2: no covariates; exposure (strategies judged helpful) and outcome (EBI) rated retrospectively by the same person; predictors chosen by significance. Describing Study 1 without a rating is reasonable.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits: 'effectiveness', 'confirming', mediation language without mediation analysis, safety claims with no safety outcome, and standardized betas read as raw slopes. The limitations are frank.

missed: The 'Acceptance and Reappraisal' count (Factor 1, 11 items) includes two responses that are the opposite of acceptance: assertively telling the experience to stop or go away (item 4, loading 0.17, kept) and directing anger or aggression at it (item 5, 0.43). It also includes questioning the challenge, journaling, breathing, closing the eyes, asking forgiveness and calling on spirits or a deity (Table 2, bold markup; Results › Study 2 › Reliability, 1st paragraph). So r = 0.50 with breakthrough is for this mixed count, not for acceptance alone, which matters for the paper's conclusion and for any claim that speaks of 'acceptance-type responses'.

Two different percentages for the same strategies should not be confused: the Descriptive statistics percentages (84.5% and so on) are of all 529 and fold together 'tried' and 'judged helpful'; how many tried each strategy but found it unhelpful is only in Fig. 1 and supplement S.VII.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 overall some concerns agreed. In the measurement domain, 'self-ratings were made blind to condition' rests on the double-blind procedure; the paper reports no check of blinding, which does not change the judgment because the two active brownies carried the same nominal THC dose.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's anxiety and sedation statement against THC alone is not supported by the Table, and the mechanism is asserted without a mediation analysis while probe-drug levels are unreported.

missed: Peak-time ranges in the Table never exceed 6.0 h although measures ran to 24 h; how long the stronger effects lasted is shown only in Figures 3 and 4 (not viewable here), so the card cannot state duration.

The many printed d intervals that include zero beside P < .05 (memory, routine tasks, PASAT, DAT, heart rate against THC alone) suggest the intervals ignore the within-person design; cite P values and means, as the card advises.
